#5830. Choosing the Initial Treatment Approach in HER2-Positive Breast Cancer

— "Beyond Diagnosis" continues with Megan Kruse on the myriad of factors that go into that decision

Developed in partnership with the Our Partner

In "Beyond Diagnosis: Early HER2-Positive Breast Cancer," Cleveland Clinic breast oncologist Megan Kruse, MD, and host John Mangels discuss how clinicians can navigate increasingly complex treatment decisions while helping patients understand their diagnosis and care.

Each installment of this series explores key aspects of early HER2-positive breast cancer care, including interpreting pathology, navigating evolving therapies, individualizing treatment, and supporting patients through shared decision-making.

In this second episode, Kruse discusses choosing between upfront surgery and neoadjuvant therapy, balancing treatment efficacy with toxicity, and tailoring treatment decisions to patients' preferences and individual circumstances.

The following is a transcript of their remarks:

Mangels: Welcome to "Beyond Diagnosis," where we talk with doctors about treatment decisions and communicating with patients. I'm your host, John Mangels. HER2-positive breast cancer is a particularly aggressive disease. Targeted therapies are improving patient treatment options, but those advances have also made care more complex.

Today, we'll explore how breast oncologists make clinical decisions, adapt treatment as new information emerges, and help patients understand their choices. Our guest is Dr. Megan Kruse. Dr. Kruse is director of breast medical oncology and co-leader of the breast cancer program at Cleveland Clinic. Dr. Kruse, thanks so much for being here.

Kruse: Thanks for having me. I'm excited about this conversation today.

Mangels: In early-stage disease, a major choice is whether treatment should begin with surgery or systemic therapy. For a patient with newly diagnosed nonmetastatic HER2-positive cancer, what features would make you lean towards surgery?

Kruse: Yeah, this is also a big topic of conversation when we first meet a patient, because I think without the HER2 knowledge, many of them come in assuming they're just going to go to surgery first because that's what happens for the vast majority of patients with breast cancer, early-stage breast cancer. So I try to explain to them that when HER2 is positive, it gives us the opportunity to give treatments before surgery to help understand how effective those treatments are.

So usually in our guidelines, we use about a 2-cm tumor as a cutoff for how large a cancer in the breast has to be to consider that preoperative chemotherapy. And any lymph node positivity generally also moves a patient into that group where we would use systemic therapy before surgery or neoadjuvant therapy, whereas the smaller tumors and negative lymph nodes, typically we would think about going to surgery first. And the reason for that really is that the intensity of the systemic therapy that we give is vastly different if you do it before surgery versus after surgery.

Mangels: What about if there is a bit of a gray area in terms of which way to go?

Kruse: Yeah, so those are our T1cN0 patients more commonly. These are tumors that are bigger than a centimeter, but less than 2 cm and node negative clinically. Those are our most challenging situations because we want to be able to personalize and adapt the systemic therapy as much as possible. And the best way to do that is to give neoadjuvant therapy, but you worry that you're being too heavy handed if you're giving these neoadjuvant regimens to patients with those smaller tumors.

And so many times I will lay that out with a patient and say, "Hey, there is some gray zone here. Here's the pluses, here's the minuses. Here's what duration of treatment would look like." Some patients really can't imagine going through 4 to 6 months of treatment with a tumor still in their body. And if that's the case and we know that we're going to make their quality of life much worse by trying to do this, maybe that pushes us one way.

These are also the great cases for tumor board again, where you say, "Hey," to your breast surgeon, "How easy do you think the surgery's going to be in the current state? Do you need me to try to shrink this tumor? Does that lymph node really look negative?" So in the gray zone cases, again, you're putting the puzzle pieces together to figure out what's the best way forward. And at the end of the day, sometimes you just have to say, "This is what my gut tells me and we're going to go with it." And most patients actually really appreciate that and they'll say, "Whatever you think is best, we should just do it."

Mangels: When neoadjuvant therapy is indicated, you as a clinician have multiple anti-HER2 agents as options. How do you weigh things like efficacy, maturity of evidence, toxicity, and patient preferences when you're making your choice?

Kruse: Yeah. It's amazing that all of those factors are going through your head at one moment in time.

Kruse: It's quite a juggling act. I would say that I come into a patient's room trying to have thought about all of this already so that I at least have my own mature sense of what I would recommend. Sometimes I go into that room and I learn about the patient and I realize I've got to flex. This plan is not going to work.

But I think when I'm coming up with that optimal plan, the first part of that is weighing largely efficacy and toxicity. When we think about these preoperative regimens in particular, the efficacy in terms of getting rid of all the cancer that you can see at the time of surgery really is our north star -- that's that pathologic complete response data point that we see in a lot of our trials. And the reason that that's so important is that pathologic complete response is an excellent surrogate for overall cancer control, overall survival, living without breast cancer recurrence.

And so when I'm looking at trials, that pathologic complete response data point is really what I'm going for because many of these trials will not have that mature survival data quite yet. But that doesn't mean I wouldn't act on that data. I'm comfortable enough with pCR (pathologic complete response) as an endpoint that we move on that.

But every improvement we've seen in pCR tends to come with some change in the side effect profile. And so that's where you have to think about which side effects are you willing to expose a certain patient to? Can they handle those? Are there long-term effects? And this is where I might view the decisions differently in a younger patient versus an older patient. Am I going to change their day-to-day functioning based on the side effects they develop? And in some of those younger patients, are there long-term consequences that if I cure them of the breast cancer, I may have to deal with a major complication 10, 15 years down the road?

So it really is a balancing act. And especially when it comes to those really long-term complications of treatment, you have to bring those up with your patients early on so that they're fully informed and that they know because some patients wouldn't be willing to take that risk. Even if it's 20% better for their cancer, they may say, "I'm not willing to worry about my heart later on." And we adapt to that.

Mangels: I'm guessing some of your patients are like, "I just want to get this tumor out of me." How do you approach and communicate with those patients that really just want to be done with the cutting part, the tumor excision part?

Kruse: Yeah. If those patients are in the gray zone based on their clinical staging, I would say we respect that decision and we may go to surgery right away. And it may change what their postsurgical systemic therapy looks like, but we still have great options. So if that is really a priority for patients, we honor that.

If there's a patient that has a larger tumor, has positive lymph nodes where I really think that neoadjuvant therapy will be important to them, I try to be as clear as possible as to why we're recommending it. And I think patients will often not realize that as we're treating with the systemic therapy that we are expecting the tumor to shrink and potentially go away. A lot of them worry that we're just getting the treatment in because we want to clear out the blood. It's really interesting that the perceptions of what chemotherapy and HER2-targeted therapy do can be all over the place when patients first come to our office.

But as you talk through that you may see this tumor shrink in real time, you may see your breasts go back to normal if it's heavier or firmer when you start treatment. And when that does happen and patients see that working, there's nothing better. They really believe in the treatment. And so being clear about what the goals are can really help with that conversation.

Mangels: It's also a learning opportunity for you as a clinician. You're seeing how that tumor responds to treatment, which is going to inform what you do going forward.

Kruse: Yeah, that's what it's all about actually. It's like an in-real-time experiment, of course an experiment that we have really excellent reasons to do. I largely tell patients that I want to know how well this treatment works on the tumor, and the only time I'm able to do that is if we still have the tumor in the breast or in the lymph nodes where we can physically feel it or see it on imaging.

Once it's cut out, we're relying on these drugs to work, but we don't really have a direct way to measure how well they're working. And actually that really resonates with patients because a lot of them want to know, did the treatment work or not? And then the counterpoint to that is if the treatment doesn't work, as disappointed as that makes all of us, it gives us an opportunity to flex after surgery and say, OK, we can use something different and try to clean up whatever may not have been killed off by the first wave of therapy.

Mangels: At the lower-risk end in patients, for example, with small node-negative tumors, how do you decide how much chemotherapy and HER2-directed therapy is adequate?

Kruse: It's a really interesting time because we're both deescalating for these low-risk patients and escalating for the higher-risk patients all at the same time. And so we're getting newer trials for these low-risk patients on a very frequent basis actually, where we're trying to remove the chemotherapy, where we're trying to lessen the number of doses of chemotherapy we're giving if we really still believe that we have to give it.

And there also are some approaches that we're using different imaging techniques to try to get a sense of really early response and escalating treatment if we're not seeing that early sign of response and then keeping the treatment lower intensity if we are seeing signs of response.

Mangels: So is that really the deciding factor for deescalation or not?

Kruse: Yeah, for the most part. If you have a lower-risk or medium-risk patient where you're still using preoperative therapy, you may see the early response as a sort of fork in the road of how intense you are with your treatment.

For those really low-risk patients where we've decided we're going to surgery first and then we're giving all of the systemic therapy after surgery, there we have a few different trial options where we can think about which particular type of chemotherapy may we want to use. Right now the conventional is HER2-targeted therapy with about 3 months of chemotherapy and then that HER2-targeted therapy continues on for the remainder of a year.

But there are some trials where we're looking at using different types of HER2-targeted therapy for various periods of time within that year to maybe have a more tolerable experience but still be really effective against the cancer.

Mangels: Are patients surprised to learn sometimes that chemotherapy doesn't have to be a part of the treatment plan?

Kruse: Absolutely, yes. And I think that...

Mangels: Surprised in a good way, I guess.

Kruse: Surprised in a good way, yeah. And we also have to do a lot of breaking down of what do these drugs actually do? What is chemotherapy? What is targeted therapy? Because many patients will assume that anything that goes in through the IV is chemo. And of course, some of our targeted therapies go through the IV, but they're not chemo and they have very different consequences for side effects, risk, how long the infusions are. And so that's a huge part of the education that we do upfront with patients.

Mangels: Chemotherapy is a familiar term with a lot of patients. Surgery, obviously people understand that, but we're talking about things like monoclonal antibodies, TKIs [tyrosine kinase inhibitors], antibody-drug conjugates. How do you explain those concepts in a way that is meaningful to patients? And do patients want to know the details of what those are or not?

Kruse: Yes, patients definitely want to know. Some are like, "OK, just give me what you think is best." But I would say most patients are wondering what the individual components of their treatment are.

Kruse: And what they do and what that means for what they can expect, or if they run into complications, which one of these are really crucial, which ones might be able to be modified or dropped. And so I typically will start with going back to that idea of HER2 being our target and which of these drugs directly go against HER2, and then which of the drugs, like chemotherapy, might affect both HER2-positive cells and general cells of the body. And that's a pretty familiar concept, like what is more specific to the cancer and what might affect my whole body.

And then when it gets into the different types of HER2-targeted medicines, monoclonal antibodies versus TKIs, monoclonal antibodies are generally IV. TKIs are generally oral. So that's kind of a nice split to explain. I don't often get into where in the cells these drugs work.

Mangels: What the effect on the receptor is.

Kruse: Right. Right. Some patients will ask that, so I'm prepared to give that information if they want it, but most patients are satisfied by saying, "OK, this is my HER2-targeted drug."

Occasionally it comes up though where you might think about using monoclonal antibodies upfront, and then if you don't have a great response, you might bring around a TKI later. And there I do find telling patients like, "Hey, this is how it works differently. One of these drugs might be more successful getting to other parts of your body, like the brain, that others would not." And actually that does resonate with them, because then they see it as, "OK, this is a way that you're helping me take care of my whole body in different ways."

Mangels: You alluded to this earlier. How do your patients' lifestyles, support systems, socioeconomic status, how do those affect the treatment decisions that you make?

Kruse: Yeah, it's huge because the best treatment plan only works if the patient's actually able to receive it and able to receive it can be so many things. It can be getting the time off of work to be able to make it to the center, having a ride to get there, having the access to supportive medications like anti-nausea medications if copays are not too high.

So I'm very fortunate that I work within a team that has multiple different providers with different levels of expertise and we can each take our part in this. So my nurse may work on one aspect of what a patient's day-to-day life is like and filling in gaps where they may not have the support at home, but maybe we have resources. Our pharmacist helps in that way as well. And our social workers are really key team members for if we can support patients during this treatment journey with different resources.

Sometimes it's education, sometimes it's personnel support like home nursing. A lot of times it's logistics, like the rides to the center. But sometimes we really do have to adjust our plans to fit whatever a patient's individual circumstances...

Mangels: I was just going to ask you, are there cases where a patient's life situation just precludes doing what you initially thought you would be doing in terms of treatment?

Kruse: Absolutely. And in those situations, you try to be creative. You try to get them the best available medication that's going to be able to fit into that lifestyle. And again, it's different for everyone. And thankfully, as the advances in the field have happened, we have more and more options that allow us to create combinations. There's a ton of data in breast cancer where we can make sure that what we're thinking about doing in a creative way is also safe. That's a huge priority, but you do have to sometimes put your thinking cap on and say, "How might we approach this?"

And again, this is a space where I rely on colleagues, where I'll present cases at tumor board because sometimes you have your blinders on and you need that fresh perspective to say, "Have you considered doing it this way?" And that's very valuable because at the end of the day, we just want to do what's best for the patients.

Mangels: Thanks so much for your insights, Dr. Kruse. And thank you for joining us on "Beyond Diagnosis," where we explore not just what physicians know, but how to effectively and compassionately share that knowledge with patients. See you next time.

#5829. At $11,995, Could This 2013 Cadillac Escalade Hybrid Make You 'Slade In The Shade?

Today's Nice Price or No Dice Cadillac Escalade is a rare Hybrid model with two electric motors sandwiched between its V8 engine and 4WD. Once very expensive, we'll have to see if this Champagne-hued luxury SUV now fits our beer budget.

For the longest time, Bentley Motors and Rolls-Royce were intrinsically intertwined, with Bentley often getting the short shrift in the partnership. In the latter half of the 20th Century, Bentley's cars often felt like an afterthought compared to the Parthenon-grilled Rolls models. That's an unfortunate bit of history, as before Rolls-Royce bought Bentley in 1931, the latter company built entire automobiles, rather than just foisting chassis and drivetrains on commissioned coachbuilders like the former.

The 1997 Bentley Brooklands we looked at on Wednesday attempted to distinguish itself from its near-twin Rolls-Royce Silver Spirit by offering a tauter suspension, toned-down body-color grille surround, and a turbocharger bolted to its 6.75-liter V8 engine. Presented in excellent condition and, in the seller's words, "needing nothing," our Bentley came with an $18,000 asking price. That's about a tenth of what the car cost new, but when it came down to brass tacks, opinions were fairly evenly split on its value. Ultimately, the brave—or foolhardy—among us lost out, as the Bentley bombed in an excruciatingly narrow 52% 'No Dice' loss.

Regardless of outcome, yesterday's Bentley was a textbook example of what the ultimate in luxury travel was intended to be in the later decades of the 20th Century. By comparison, the 2013 Cadillac Escalade Hybrid that comes our way today is a more modern execution of that concept.

The Escalade, of course, is the vehicle that arguably saved Cadillac. Originally a slapped-together version of the GMC Denali SUV, the Escalade proved so successful that GM added additional versions and further differentiation with later iterations. Those included the comically weird ESV version based on the Chevy Avalanche pickup. One of the rarest Escalade models is the initial 4WD Hybrid, produced between 2009 and 2013.

The Hybrid Escalade's party piece is the dual-mode AHS2 (Advanced Hybrid System 2, Electric Boogaloo), which replaces the traditional automatic transmission. Co-developed by GM, Daimler-Chrysler, and BMW, the hybrid drive unit was used in several of GM's SUVs, along with Mercedes and BMW sedans and the Dodge Durango. Dual mode means the truck can be powered by the gasoline engine, one of the 60-kilowatt electric motors, or a combination of both. Another 60kW electric motor serves as a generator for the nickel-metal hydride battery pack. This was technology that all three partners in the development consortium thought would pave the way to greater efficiency, but ultimately proved overly complicated for the task. All three dropped the hybrid drive unit by the end of the 2013 model year.

This Escalade Hybrid is one result of that short-lived partnership and product run. According to the ad, it has done 140,000 miles (132k according to the text, 140k according to the sidebar listing details — we'll go with the larger number) and, aside from some minor wear and tear, presents admirably for those miles.

Naturally, the most expensive component of any hybrid or fully electric vehicle is the battery, and it's reassuring to know the pack in this Escalade was replaced at 90K. That gives it at least another 40K if the current pack has the same lifespan as the first.

On the gas side of things, there's a 6.0-liter LZ1 V8, making 332 horsepower and 367 pound-feet of torque all by its lonesome. Specs indicate that, combined with the electric motors, power jumps to 379 horses.

Per the seller, the HV battery isn't the only new component this truck has seen. It also has new shocks and suspension components, refreshed brake pads, and new tires on its chrome-plated factory alloys. The ad claims no issues with the truck's performance, saying that it has been "extremely well maintained with all the expensive items already taken care of."

Overall, the truck looks as nice as its description lets on. The exterior, appropriately enough in metallic Champagne, is said to only suffer from some minor scuffs on the rear bumper cap. Other than that, it still shines and is matched with clear, unclouded headlamp covers.

The interior looks lived-in but far from abused. The leather on the driver's seat has the patina of many posteriors, but seems fully intact. So too does the leather on the steering wheel, albeit with a glossy sheen expected given the truck's age and miles. The only other really glaring issue is the wear evident on the fan control in the automatic climate control panel. Geez, people, just leave it on auto!

This is a three-row SUV with room for seven, so it should be as versatile as it is efficient. It comes with built-in navigation, a tow package, and, most importantly, a clean title.

When new, this Escalade commanded over $77,000 to drive it off the dealership lot. That was a long time ago, with many miles and a long-expired warranty in the rearview, so naturally it should cost less now. We need to decide whether the seller's set price of $11,995 is low enough.

Since this one comes with the promise that all the expensive work is already done, it may be a safe bet to take ownership. Also, I think the less said about the AI-generated image of the truck in the ad as some sort of weird road boat, the better.

What do you say? Is this rare hybrid Escalade worth $11,995 as it sits? Or is that too much for a truck with an abandoned technology, no matter how fancy it is?

#5828. Electric Buses Need a Plan for the Next Operating Contract

Greater Manchester is entering a new stage of bus franchising. In September 2026, Go-Ahead announced that Go North West had won two Bee Network operating contracts covering 38 routes and approximately 60 buses, with service beginning in March 2027. Eighteen of those routes will operate from a new depot in Leigh. The award is a reminder that operating companies can change while the depots, charging infrastructure and grid connections supporting the passenger network remain in place for decades.

Electric-bus procurement adds a long-lived physical commitment to contracts that are often much shorter. An operating agreement may run for five to seven years. A depot building, substation or multi-megawatt electricity connection can remain useful through several such contracts. Buses can sometimes be transferred between operators, but land, cable routes, electrical capacity and installed charging equipment are tied to particular sites. Those assets need to support the passenger service even when the company responsible for driving the buses changes.

Consider an authority retendering electric-bus routes. The incumbent has used a convenient depot and financed chargers and a substantial grid connection. A competing operator submits an attractive price and a credible operating plan, but has no assured right to use the depot and electricity infrastructure. It might need to negotiate with the incumbent, find alternative premises or secure another grid connection, potentially adding years of work and substantial costs. A nominally competitive tender can become much less contestable once those obligations are included.

South Yorkshire has taken a deliberate approach to this problem. In March 2026, the South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority announced the purchase of five major depots, adding them to the publicly owned Leger Way depot in Doncaster. First Bus and Stagecoach will lease the acquired premises back during the transition. The authority intends to use the estate for franchised operations and electric-bus infrastructure, with its first franchised services scheduled for September 2027. Six operators reached the next procurement stage for the initial packages at Olive Grove and Leger Way.

This does not establish that every city should own every depot. London has long maintained a publicly specified, competitively operated bus network while many garages remain outside direct Transport for London ownership. Secure leases, access rights, assignable contracts and specialist infrastructure providers may preserve the same continuity, depending on the local market. The practical test is whether a qualified successor operator can obtain the depot, buses, charging capacity and operational information required to take over on the contracted date.

Remaining asset value is central to that test. If an operator finances twenty-year charging infrastructure under a five-year contract, it needs to know what happens to the investment if another operator wins the routes. The authority must also avoid paying for a useful electrical connection and then finding it cannot make that capacity available to the next contractor. Depreciation, compensation, asset transfer, warranties, software access and grid-connection permissions need to be settled before the first contract ends, ideally before it starts.

England’s January 2026 bus-franchising guidance recognizes the importance of depots, charging infrastructure, transfer arrangements and competition in subsequent procurements. The engineering of electric buses has advanced considerably. Public authorities now need procurement structures that keep the fleet and its supporting infrastructure useful as routes, contractors and technologies evolve.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing article examines the second-contract test through Greater Manchester and South Yorkshire, including asset access, residual values and operating continuity. It draws on my open report, The Bus Is Not the System, comparing metropolitan bus governance and electrification across Britain and Ireland.

#5827. Two New Commissioners Headed to the Arizona Corporation Commission

Phoenix — Come January, the Arizona Corporation Commission (ACC) will be bi-partisan as two Democrats, Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill, have been elected to the ACC. They will be joining current Republican commissioners Lea Márquez Peterson, Rachel Walden, and René Lopez. The election comes as the Commission is considering rate increases for Arizona Public Service Company (APS) and Tucson Electric Power Company (TEP), and mechanisms that would allow both utilities to increase rates every year with less stakeholder input, and as the Commission begins to consider the utilities’ proposed long-term resource plans.

As a recent Sierra Club report makes clear, the ACC wields a tremendous amount of power over the future of Arizona’s energy landscape, public health, and utility bill increases, especially as the state experiences a fossil gas rush to power data centers. Arizonans experience some of the highest electric bills in the country, with some of the most planned gas in the country and with Arizona’s largest utility, APS, opting to run the dirty Four Corners coal plant for more than another decade. Yet, up until now, the Commission has made a habit of increasing ratepayer bills, opting for expensive fossil fuels and cutting programs that require utilities to utilize solar energy to generate electricity and to conserve energy, lower electric bills, and invest in energy efficiency.

In response, Sierra Club Grand Canyon Chapter Director Sandy Bahr issued the following statement:

“These election results should act as a wakeup call to the rest of the Arizona Corporation Commission. Arizonans are tired of being put on the backburner, bearing the burden for expensive fossil fuels that harm our neighbors and contribute to climate change. We share in the optimism of our fellow voters and will continue to carefully monitor the ACC as our work to promote clean air, clean water, and healthy communities and a healthy climate enters a new chapter.”

The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. In addition to protecting every person's right to get outdoors and access the healing power of nature, the Sierra Club works to promote clean energy, safeguard the health of our communities, protect wildlife, and preserve our remaining wild places through grassroots activism, public education, lobbying, and legal action. #5826. Kimi Antonelli Won The F1 Driver's Championship On A Cracked Oil Sump

Twenty-year-old Kimi Antonelli made history on Sunday becoming the youngest Formula 1 Drivers' Champion in the history of the sport and the first Italian driver to win it since Alberto Ascari in 1953. He clinched it finishing third at last weekend's Mexico Grand Prix, sharing the podium with fellow champs and legends in their own rights, Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, who lifted Antonelli up onto their shoulders for an F1 photo op to end all F1 photo ops.

Mathematically, Antonelli's championship win was almost a foregone conclusion at that point, but his picture-perfect victory almost didn't happen that way because it's now been revealed that his final laps in Mexico City were done in a car that was very much on its last legs. Mercedes F1 deputy team principal Bradley Lord appeared on the High Performance Racing podcast after Sunday's race and said Antonelli won it all on a cracked oil sump.

"We got the car back after the race, took the floor off the bottom — covered in oil," Lord recalled. "Sump cracked, and Kimi said he thinks about four laps from the end, he could start to feel the engine just starting to struggle. So, right on the edge of retirement of that race and yet it held together." For what it's worth, non-catastrophic engine issues were a bit of a theme for Mercedes in Mexico as Antonelli's teammate George Russell, who qualified P2, suffered a power unit "deployment problem" right at the start of the race. He lost multiple places quickly and eventually finished sixth.

Cracked sump or not, it's unlikely Antonelli would've been going ham in those final stages of his race anyway as he apparently struggled to even see through his own tears before crossing the finish line as World Champion, according to Sky Sports. In the end, he finished a little over four seconds away from second-place Hamilton, who was eight-tenths off of race winner Verstappen. The Italian driver picked up 15 points, more than enough to secure the biggest trophy in motorsport earlier in life than anybody else who'd ever done it before.

#5825. What's The Worst Road Trip You've Ever Taken?

It might be getting colder outside, but road trips aren't over for the year yet. The busiest driving days are the days around Thanksgiving and Christmas, as people travel to visit loved ones. Some might be just heading across town. Others are driving around the state, while others are traveling across the country. And while the old adage that "it's not about the destination, it's about the journey" might be true, the journey can be crummy. What's the worst road trip you've ever taken?

Plenty of things can spoil a long drive. Snow is on the way in the next few months, and that's always something to look out for, but with hurricane season winding down, you can still get caught in a torrential downpour or an early winter storm with lots of non-frozen water. Never underestimate how dangerous precipitation can be out on the road. I learned that lesson the hard way while driving across Pennsylvania before the start of a fall semester in college. It was raining so hard that I couldn't see beyond my hood. The curtain of water made visibility so poor that I had to pull over beneath an underpass for shelter.

A big part of driving for hours at a time is staying comfortable behind the wheel. When it's scorching hot outside, a good climate control system is the only thing that can keep you cool inside a car because rolling down the windows will literally just blow hot air into your face. If an issue crops up with your car's air conditioning unit, it's never an easy fix. A road trip, especially a summer one, where your air conditioning breaks can be particularly brutal. You either have to suffer through oppressive temperatures, or stop somewhere unfamiliar to get a fix — potentially delaying your trip quite a bit.

A bad road trip could be well outside the bounds of one that's got expensive repairs or uncomfortable conditions. It could be an ultra-long trip that goes exclusively past boring, endless, flat terrain with no music to keep you entertained.

You tell us what your idea of a bad road trip is by leaving the story of your worst road trip in the comment section below. Include all the aggravating details along with the pertinent information, like when and where you were driving.

#5824. Child Dies of Measles in Wisconsin's First Such Death Since 1990

— Four measles-associated deaths confirmed by CDC this year, but states report higher numbers

An infant in southwestern Wisconsin has died after contracting measles, the state's first death from the disease in 36 years, state officials announced Thursday.

The coroner listed the cause of death as measles, state health officials said.

"My heart is broken for the family," said Kirsten Johnson, MPH, secretary of the state health department. "Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease."

The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.

The CDC has confirmed four measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. In Pennsylvania alone, health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.

As of Thursday, Wisconsin reported 431 cases of measles, all but three in unvaccinated people. Nine people had been hospitalized.

#5823. Hyundai Motor Group Outlines Future Mobility Technology Roadmap at FISITA World Mobility Summit 2026

HWASEONG, Korea — Hyundai Motor Group (the Group) is co-hosting the FISITA World Mobility Summit 2026 with the International Federation of Automotive Engineering Societies (FISITA). The two-day summit is taking place Nov. 4–5 at Rolling Hills Hotel in Hwaseong, Korea.

Founded in 1948, FISITA is a global organization that brings together automotive engineering societies and industry experts to promote knowledge exchange and technological innovation in automotive engineering. It holds the World Mobility Summit every two years, bringing together executives and technology leaders from global mobility companies to discuss industry challenges and future technology directions, such as artificial intelligence (AI) and vehicle electrification.

This year’s summit is the first to be held in Korea. Chang Hwan Kim, Executive Vice President and Head of the Electrification Energy Solutions Tech Unit at Hyundai Motor Group, is the first Korean to serve as FISITA President.

“Hyundai Motor Group will continue to strengthen its competitiveness in key future mobility technologies and continue to participate in technology exchange and collaboration across the global automotive industry to contribute to the development of the future mobility sector.” –Chang Hwan Kim, Executive Vice President and Head of the Electrification Energy Solutions Tech Unit at Hyundai Motor Group

On the first day, Manfred Harrer, President and Head of R&D Division at Hyundai Motor Group, delivered a keynote address introducing the Group’s electrification strategy. It encompasses battery electric vehicles (BEVs), hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs) and fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs). Harrer described the Group’s technology development roadmap for responding flexibly to market changes and customer needs.

Harrer also emphasized strengthening future vehicle development capabilities by combining engineering technology with AI-based digital capabilities and connecting the strengths of different technologies to pursue a sustainable mobility future.

In his opening remarks, Kim said that the automotive industry is undergoing an unprecedented technological transition. He emphasized that diverse technology approaches and stronger global collaboration are important to the advancement of future mobility.

Under the theme “Embracing the Complexities of Mobility,” the summit is addressing key technologies and challenges facing the automotive industry, including software-defined vehicles (SDVs), AI, autonomous driving, batteries and energy infrastructure.

Executives and technology leaders from across the global automotive industry are in attendance, sharing perspectives on key technology challenges and future development directions for the mobility industry.

Keynotes and panel discussions are examining major changes in the automotive industry, including advances in AI and software, the evolution of autonomous driving technology and the diversification of electrification technologies. Participants are also discussing technology directions and ways for the industry to collaborate in response to these shifts.

Major automakers are presenting vehicle and technology exhibits during the summit. The Group is displaying the Genesis GV90 and Hyundai TUCSON, along with a battery pack, hydrogen tank and robotics platform.

#5822. Here Are All The Cool Cars Elon Musk Could Have Bought Instead Of Spending $474,000,000 On Political Ads

The midterm elections are over. If you live in a swing state like I do, you've probably been inundated with political attack ads, texts, and phone calls for the last several months. This has been the most expensive election in U.S. history, and much of the blame for that can be laid on the shoulders of the richest man in the world, and one-time Jalopnik contributor, Elon Musk. After Joe Biden spurned him in 2021, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has become the single largest political donor in history, spending hundreds of millions of dollars in support of Republican political campaigns. According to recent reports Musk spent an incredible 474 million American greenbacks nationwide, with some $200 million of that spent supporting Ken Paxton's campaign for U.S. Senate in his adopted home state of Texas.

Megadonor Musk's efforts were all in vain as every one of the political campaigns he supported in swing states failed. With economic inequality, an incredibly unpopular war, and AI data centers among the top concerns for American voters in this election, it certainly feels like these results are a referendum on Musk himself. Musk spent the weeks leading up to the election using his social media platform Twitter to call Texas Senator Elect James Talarico a "far left extremist" when he wasn't using it to promote his AI chatbot or retweet the thoughts of vile bigots.

So, after all that, it seems the world's only trillionaire decided to throw away half a billion dollars on unelectable candidates and an extremely unpopular agenda. $474 million is a small fraction of Elon's net worth, just under half a tenth of a percent, in fact. He probably won't even notice the money is gone, but the fact remains that he could have spent that money instead on something much cooler. He could have bought 6,423 brand new base model Corvettes, for example. He could have given each of the 500 people living in SpaceX company town Starbase, Texas, 12 Corvettes as a gift.

What if he had grander ambitions than Corvettes? Let's look into it.

Back in August, if Musk had found himself at Monterey Car Week instead of pumping money into his super pacs, he could have really cleaned house and built himself a really cool collection of some of the most important cars in history. As the CEO of the world's most valuable car company, Musk must have at least some interest in cars, right? He did own a McLaren F1 at one point, for example, so maybe there is still a car guy hiding in there. Auction house RM Sotheby's recently set a record for collector car auctions in Monterey, with more money changing hands that weekend than ever had in history. The wealthy car collectors are still flush with cash and willing to spend, it seems. The sale was led by the controversial $40 million Ferrari Luce charity auction, a rare $34.655 million McLaren F1 GTR sale, and an $18.7 million 1963 Corvette Grand Sport. In total the auction pushed 199 lots across the dais and nearly half of them were million-plus sales. What was that record breaking number? $380 million, meaning Musk could have used his political contribution slush fund to buy every single one of them and still have money left over for transportation, taxes, and registration.

If Musk really wants to be as popular as it seems he is desperate to be, he could have spent the summer driving around in his new Aston Martin Valkyrie Spider, Talbot-Lago T26 Record Cabriolet, Mercer Raceabout, or Lamborghini Miura P400. The point is, he could have bought whatever he wanted, but instead of something cool or useful, what he wanted was Ken Paxton.

What if he wanted to own the most expensive collector cars of all time? For just the money he spent in Texas he could easily have bought the one-of-two Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR "Uhlenhaut Coupe" which sold in 2022 for $142,000,000. In fact, for his 2026 political campaign contributions, Musk could have also purchased the Mercedes-Benz W 196 R Stromlinienwagen ($52,960,000), a Ferrari 330 LM/250 GTO ($51,705,000), another 250 GTO ($48,405,000), a Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe ($42,905,000), the aforementioned Ferrari Luce, and yet two more Ferrari 250 GTOs ($38,500,000 and $38,115,000 respectively). That's the top eight most expensive cars ever sold in history. Or, you know, one feckless midterm election media buy blitz. Which would you rather have?

Let's say Elon woke up one day and felt like he wanted to do something magnanimous in an effort to repair his reputation with the American people. What could he have done with his $474,000,000 political contributions that would have instead helped the average American feel better about their country and place in it? Auto loan debt is pretty bad right now, reaching some $1.7 trillion. Obviously he couldn't clear the table on every car loan, and it would be absurd to expect him to. That said, Texas has been hit harder by auto loan debt than any other state with around 10% of borrowers in the state more than 30 days behind on their payments. How much goodwill could he garner for himself and Tesla if he were to forgive all Tesla loans in the state? That might be a good start.

Half a billion dollars buys a whole lot of goodwill for a man. Maybe he could start subsidizing grocery stores in poor Texas neighborhoods. Or pushing to fund the state's unreliable and undermaintained power grid. He could set up a fund to install EV chargers in apartment complexes or on the street, further growing Tesla's potential customer base in the state. Man, there are just so many better uses of that money than attack ads claiming James Talarico isn't manly enough to represent Texas.

My biggest takeaway from this election cycle is that America's wealthiest donor is spending his tremendous wealth trying to buy politicians. Thankfully, this time anyway, it seems that the voters have rebuked that effort. It certainly should be one of the priorities of this new crop of elected representatives to remove the ability for one man to wield this much potential political power, regardless of whether it was successful or not. It seems Americans are desperate for some kind of financial relief, whether that's reducing gas prices by ending the war in Iran, combating inflation, or making healthcare affordable, rather than fighting ridiculous culture wars. While those should be major priorities for the Democrats, campaign finance reform should probably be on the docket somewhere.

Elon seems to have made himself incredibly unpopular across the last half decade simply by aligning himself with MAGA Republicans. He's going to have a long uphill battle to revamp his image. Maybe he should just disappear from public life for a decade or so. Or buy a few hundred vintage collector cars at auction and simply give them to random American car enthusiasts. Either way, he should probably stop tweeting.

#5821. You Need A New Car? Go Electric! It’s Superior Technology! Part 1

Your car is getting “long in tooth,” or maybe your daughter is going away to college and you are giving her your car. Whatever the reason, you are looking for another car. It could be new, it could be used: don’t even look at gas cars, electric cars are superior technology!

The wheels on every railroad locomotive in the world are driven by electric motors. All the busiest rail routes in Europe and China are pure electric, including high-speed rail. 98% of new cars in Norway are electric, over 80% of new cars in Denmark are electric. In China, the country with the largest sales of new cars in the world, the percentage of new electric cars in September 2026 was 67%. 82% of the operating bus fleet in China is electric. Even ships and airplanes are going electric. The data is unequivocal: electric propulsion is superior to internal combustion propulsion. Only the huge political contributions to Trump by the fossil fuel industry and his resulting anti-EV policies have slowed down adoption in this country.

In places we’ve been like California; Portland, Oregon; and northern Utah, you are seeing a lot of Teslas, so you know that electric cars are working for a lot of people these days. It’s time for you to do some research on electric cars.

You do pay a premium for new electric cars, because the batteries are still quite expensive. If price is the driving factor for you, buy a used electric car. Hardly any used EVs are high mileage, and EV batteries still have plenty of life even after they go off warranty at 8 years and 120,000 miles. There are thousands of lightly used EVs sitting at used car lots at reasonable prices all over the country these days. Some used car dealers will give you an estimate of the battery life. If not, get a friend who is an experienced EV driver to help you evaluate the battery life of the EV you are considering.

If you just do local driving or have two cars and have a garage or off-street parking, an EV is a no brainer. EVs are hands-down more convenient than gas cars for local driving. Your EV will have plenty of range for local driving, it will get a complete charge overnight in your home garage refueling station and it will never need an oil change.

EVs are as quiet as mice, as smooth as kittens, and as quick as jackrabbits. They have simple electric motors, not complex internal combustion engines. They have simple one-speed transmissions, not complex 7-speed automatic transmissions. They don’t have exhaust systems with mufflers that will rust and need replacement. They don’t have emission control systems with limited life. They don’t have complex cooling systems with big radiators. You seldom use your brakes with an EV, so your brakes may last the life of the car. They don’t have a big lead-acid battery for starting, with a maximum life of 5 years. New EVs have only a small lithium-ion battery, which lasts 10+ years. Bottom line: Routine maintenance for EVs is almost nil. I think the only real maintenance item on a Tesla over the first 3 years is the cabin air filter. You can expect an EV to go 500,000 miles without major repair or replacement in most cases.

Perhaps you can stomach buying a car from Tesla whose CEO has become one of the most despicable persons on the planet lately. (Example: Musk recently suspended access to his Starlink communications system to the Ukrainians who are valiantly defending their country from the Russian aggressors.) However, Tesla has sold almost 10 million automobiles worldwide that don’t emit CO2 and particulate pollution while operating. Tesla also has by far the most ubiquitous charging system, which allows cross-country driving on major US roads with little planning. Consider buying a Tesla.

So, what about cross-country trips? Everyone knows that long-distance trips in an electric car are inconvenient or even impossible, because there aren’t enough charging stations and it takes an hour if you can find one. Wrong: Every 100 miles along all the major Interstate highways, Tesla has built Superchargers with 8 to 32 and a few with over 100 charging stalls. By the time you have gone to the bathroom, walked the dog, and chatted with a fellow EV owner for a few minutes, you probably have more than enough charge to continue your journey. Usually, charging takes about 20 minutes. If you need a longer charge, you may need to watch a bit of Octopus Teacher or Back to the Future II on the big screen in the car for another 10 minutes.

News flash! Since February 28, 2023, most Tesla Superchargers (now North American Charging Standard/NACS chargers) are usable by all EV brands. Unfortunately, older Tesla Superchargers can’t be used by other brands, so I would still advise buying a Tesla if you want carefree cross-country driving. CCS chargers which are native to most other brands have sprung up by the thousands in the US, which together with the newer Tesla Superchargers make it possible to travel cross-country with non-Teslas on many routes with some planning. Also, Teslas can use non-Tesla chargers. Non-Tesla chargers often come with Tesla cables now, so Tesla owners don’t even need an adapter in most cases. However, even Teslas require careful planning if you are driving far from major highways.

My wife and I have done cross-country trips from Utah to Wisconsin for 7 years, on to North Carolina (once), and back to Utah. We have also traveled from Utah to Southern California at the same 500 miles per day rate that we used to do with our gas cars … and with no worries, mate.

I’m going to try to pass on some things I’ve learned from driving five different electric vehicles over 12 years and some 200,000 miles. See part two, coming soon.

If you find any of my articles helpful to you, please use my referral link when buying a new Tesla: https://ts.la/arthur73734 (Be sure to use it when you make your order). Tesla keeps changing the program, but here’s the latest: If you are buying a new Tesla Model 3 or Y and use my link, you will get two months of free Full Self Driving (a ~$200 value) on top of the one month that comes free with every new Model Y right now. This will get you a total of 3 months free Full Self Driving. It will be $99/month after that. For a Cybertruck, you will get $1000 off your purchase price. At this moment, Tesla is offering a year of free Supercharging with the purchase of a new Model 3 Premium or Performance.

#5820. Patients Want 'Deep Plane' Facelifts. Are They Actually Better?

— Plastic surgeons weigh in on different rhytidectomy techniques

Welcome to Culture Clinic, MedPage Today's collaboration with Northwell Health to offer a healthcare professional's take on the latest viral medical topics.

As elective plastic surgery procedures, including facelifts, become more popular among everyday Americans, plastic surgeons say more people come in requesting "deep plane" facelifts.

Aviva Preminger, MD, a spokesperson for the American Society of Plastic Surgeons, has experienced this in her own practice in New York City. Whereas historically patients would come in asking for a facelift, now they ask for deep plane facelifts specifically.

"I think that the deep plane facelift is really having a moment right now, especially because of social media," Preminger told MedPage Today.

Indeed, there's been ample speculation online -- including from plastic surgeons -- about Kris Jenner, guessing that she's had a deep plane facelift.

While there's more awareness about deep plane facelifts, there's also some simmering misinformation, Preminger cautioned, noting that "social media can sometimes create the impression that one technique is universally superior for everyone," which isn't the case.

Deep plane facelifts aren't new; the procedure was first described by plastic surgeon Sam Hamra, MD, in 1990. Unlike traditional superficial facelifts, deep plane facelifts go below the superficial musculoaponeurotic system, which is the fibromuscular layer that supports the facial soft tissues.

"By releasing certain retaining ligaments, the surgeon can actually mobilize and reposition the deeper tissues of the cheeks, jawline, and the lower face, with the goal being to restore a more youthful facial contour without placing too much tension on the skin," Preminger said. Essentially, the intent of this procedure is "to address the deeper structural layers of the face rather than simply tightening the skin," she added.

Both traditional and deep plane facelifts involve incisions by the ears and at the hairline, but the exact position depends on skin laxity.

Lyle Leipziger, MD, chief of plastic surgery at Northwell Health's North Shore University Hospital in Manhasset, New York, and Long Island Jewish Medical Center in New Hyde Park, New York, told MedPage Today that deep plane facelifts are most appropriate for the mid-face, but there are a lot of considerations, like skin texture and tone, how a patient looked when they were younger, and how their face has sagged with age.

Because deep plane facelifts involve both tightening and repositioning, the results should be long-lasting. But Leipziger emphasized that one technique isn't superior to the other; it's a matter of choosing the appropriate strategy for a patient's facial structure and aesthetic goals.

Both traditional and deep plane facelifts should have longevity, he noted, but a consultation with an experienced surgeon is vital. That way, the surgeon can have an open conversation with the patient setting realistic expectations.

"You shouldn't choose a facelift based on the name of the technique alone," Leipziger said. "The technique really should be tailored to the face and not the other way around."

Depending on a patient's goals, Preminger said that it's not uncommon for surgeons to combine facelifts with other facial procedures. It used to be the case that patients were told to expect their facelift to last about 10 years, she added, but plastic surgery has improved greatly. Patients' genetics, sun exposure, and weight loss all impact the longevity of results, but patients now have access to non-surgical maintenance, like laser resurfacing, botulinum toxin (Botox), and filler, which add to the procedure's longevity.

Preminger said that facelifts aren't particularly painful, but innovation in the plastic surgery space still makes for better experiences. She noted that tranexamic acid can help reduce bruising, hemostatic nets can help reduce swelling and avoid the use of drains, and suzetrigine (Journavx) is a non-narcotic working well for post-op pain control.

More than anything, this trend reflects a broader cultural shift where plastic surgery is no longer thought of as a luxury only for the rich and famous but as an option for anyone willing to pay for it, surgeons said.
